signs: User input joined or pasted into SQL text (+, f-strings, template strings, string concatenation).
Column or table names taken from the request (ORDER BY, sort fields), which parameters can't cover.
Values from your own database that someone else once typed in (second-order injection).
fixes: Use parameters or placeholders for every value.
For names (columns, directions), choose from a fixed allowlist.
Turn values into the type you expect (an int, a date) before they reach the query.

example.bad: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'")

decoys.fix: Remove single quotes from the input before building the query.
decoys.why: Numbers, column names and other contexts need no quotes, and escaping by hand misses cases. Parameters are the only reliable fix.

decoys.fix: Check the input isn't empty and is shorter than 100 characters.
decoys.why: ' OR 1=1 -- is short and not empty. Length checks don't stop SQL being changed.

decoys.fix: Run the query with a read-only database user.
decoys.why: That limits damage but the attacker can still read every row. The query itself must stop treating input as SQL.

signs: User text written into HTML without escaping (echo, innerHTML, template strings).
Text placed inside attributes, <script> blocks or URLs, where HTML escaping isn't enough.
Filters that remove <script> or < only, instead of encoding for the place the text goes.
fixes: Escape for the context: HTML text, attribute, JavaScript or URL each need their own encoding.
Use a template engine that escapes by default, and allow only http(s) links.
Add a Content Security Policy as a second line of defence.

decoys.fix: Remove <script> tags from the text before showing it.
decoys.why: Event handlers like onerror, javascript: links and attribute breakouts need no script tag.

decoys.fix: Only show the text to signed-in users.
decoys.why: Signed-in users are exactly the victims: the script runs in their session.

decoys.fix: Check the text on the browser side before it's submitted.
decoys.why: Attackers send requests directly. Anything the browser checks can be skipped.

signs: An ID from the address or body used to load a record, with no check of who owns it.
Checks that prove who you are (signed in, has a role) but not what you may touch.
Roles or permissions read from the request instead of from the server's own records.
fixes: Filter every query by the signed-in user (or check the owner) on the server.
Check permission for the specific object, not just the route.
Read roles from the database or session, never from what the client sends.

decoys.fix: Use long random IDs so nobody can guess another user's record.
decoys.why: IDs leak in links, logs and screenshots. Hard-to-guess IDs slow attackers down but don't check permission.

decoys.fix: Hide the link to other users' records in the app.
decoys.why: The API still answers. Attackers call it directly with any ID.

decoys.fix: Require users to be signed in for this endpoint.
decoys.why: Being signed in proves who you are, not that the record is yours.

signs: Keys, passwords or tokens written in code, config files or app bundles.
"Fallback" values like os.environ.get('KEY', 'dev-secret') that end up in production.
Secret keys used from a mobile app or browser, where anyone can read them.
fixes: Keep secrets in a secret manager or the server's environment, and fail to start without them.
Never ship server secrets in apps: the app calls your server, which holds the key.
Rotate any secret that was ever committed, then remove it from history.

example.good: const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY; // set on the server, never committed

decoys.fix: Split the key into two strings and join them at run time.
decoys.why: Anyone reading the code (or the app) can join them too.

decoys.fix: Make the repository private.
decoys.why: Private repos get cloned, leaked and shared with contractors, and app bundles are public anyway.

decoys.fix: Encode the key in base64 so it isn't readable.
decoys.why: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Decoding it takes a second.

signs: Passwords or PINs hashed with fast hashes: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 on their own.
No salt, or too few iterations for a slow hash.
Passwords encrypted (reversible) instead of hashed.
fixes: Use Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt (or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count).
Let the library handle salts, and compare with its verify function.
For short PINs, also limit attempts on the server, because any hash of 10,000 PINs can be brute-forced.

decoys.fix: Hash the password twice with SHA-256.
decoys.why: Two fast hashes are still fast. Attackers try billions of guesses a second.

decoys.fix: Store the hash in a separate database table.
decoys.why: Whoever steals one table usually steals them all. The hash itself has to be slow.

decoys.fix: Encrypt passwords with AES-256 instead.
decoys.why: Encryption can be undone with the key. Passwords must be stored so nobody can read them back.

signs: File names from users joined onto a folder path (including names inside zip files).
Filters that remove ../ once, or check text with startsWith without a trailing separator.
Downloads or uploads that take a path or file name from the request.
fixes: Resolve the full path and check it stays inside the folder (compare with folder + separator).
Better still, look files up by ID and never use the user's name as a path.
Use helpers like send_from_directory or basename where they fit.

decoys.fix: Replace "../" with nothing in the file name.
decoys.why: ....// becomes ../ after one pass, and encoded or absolute paths get through.

decoys.fix: Only allow file names that end in .pdf.
decoys.why: ../other-folder/secret.pdf still ends in .pdf.

decoys.fix: Run the app as a user that can't read /etc/passwd.
decoys.why: It can still read everything the app can: other users' files, keys and config.

signs: The server fetches a URL that a user supplied (logos, webhooks, imports, previews).
Blocklists of 'localhost' or text checks (startsWith, endsWith) on the URL.
Redirects followed after the check, or DNS answers that change.
fixes: Allow only the hosts you need, or resolve and refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses at connect time.
Don't follow redirects (or check each one), and allow only https.
Run fetchers where they can't reach internal services or cloud metadata.

decoys.fix: Block URLs that contain "localhost" or "127.0.0.1".
decoys.why: 169.254.169.254, 10.x addresses, other spellings of 127.0.0.1 and DNS names pointing inside all get through.

decoys.fix: Only accept URLs that start with https://.
decoys.why: Internal services and some metadata endpoints are reachable over https too, and redirects can lead anywhere.

decoys.fix: Set a 5 second timeout on the request.
decoys.why: Timeouts limit slow requests. They don't stop fast ones to internal addresses.

signs: pickle, PHP unserialize, Java ObjectInputStream, YAML full loaders or similar on data from outside.
Cookies, uploads or queues that carry serialised objects.
Options that look like hardening but allow all classes.
fixes: Use a data-only format: JSON, or YAML with safe_load.
If objects must be restored, sign the data and allow only specific classes.
Validate the structure after parsing.

decoys.fix: Base64 encode the data so it can't be tampered with.
decoys.why: Base64 is just an encoding. Anyone can decode, change and re-encode it.

decoys.fix: Check the result is a dictionary after loading it.
decoys.why: The attack runs while loading, before your check ever sees the result.

decoys.fix: Only accept data under 256 KB.
decoys.why: Exploit payloads are tiny. Size limits don't help.

signs: Amounts, quantities or counts used without checking their range (negative, zero, fractions, huge).
Checks for only one side of a range, or comparisons that miss earlier activity (total refunded so far).
Formats (phone numbers, dates, IDs) accepted without checking.
fixes: Validate type, range and format on the server, for every business rule.
Use whole units (kobo) as integers and check both ends of the range.
Re-check limits against totals inside the same database transaction.

example.good: if (!Number.isInteger(amount) || amount <= 0 || amount > balance) return error();

decoys.fix: Validate the amount in the app's form before it's sent.
decoys.why: Attackers send requests directly. Only server-side checks count.

decoys.fix: Round the amount to two decimal places.
decoys.why: -5000.00 is still negative. Rounding doesn't enforce the rule.

decoys.fix: Log every transfer so you can find abuse later.
decoys.why: Logs help after the money is gone. The rule has to be enforced before.

signs: Error messages, stack traces, SQL or file paths sent to the client.
Debug switches that a request can turn on (a query string, a header).
Database error text (constraint names, values) passed straight through.
fixes: Log the details on the server with a reference, and return a plain message and that reference.
Turn debug output off by configuration, never by request.
Map known errors (like duplicates) to fixed, friendly messages.

decoys.fix: Only show the stack trace to users who are signed in.
decoys.why: Anyone can sign up. Internal details help attackers whoever sees them.

decoys.fix: Shorten the error message to its first 100 characters.
decoys.why: The first line of a database error is usually the most revealing part.

decoys.fix: Return status 200 so errors look like successes.
decoys.why: It hides problems from monitoring and still leaks whatever text is returned.

signs: PINs, passwords, card numbers or tokens in SharedPreferences, UserDefaults, plain files or SQLite.
Sensitive files written to shared or public storage (Downloads, Documents).
Secure storage used for one value while another copy sits in plain storage.
fixes: Don't store what you don't need (PINs, full card numbers, CVVs).
Use the Keystore/Keychain (EncryptedSharedPreferences, flutter_secure_storage) for tokens.
Keep files in the app's private storage and share them with a FileProvider.

example.good: // Never store the PIN; ask for it, or use BiometricPrompt

decoys.fix: Use MODE_PRIVATE so other apps can't read the file.
decoys.why: Root, backups and malware with root still read plain files. Sensitive values need encryption, or no storage at all.

decoys.fix: Base64 encode the value before saving it.
decoys.why: Base64 isn't encryption. It's undone instantly.

decoys.fix: Clear the stored value when the user signs out.
decoys.why: It's exposed the whole time they're signed in, and on any backup taken meanwhile.

signs: Certificate checks switched off (badCertificateCallback, trust-all managers, hostname verifiers that return true).
Cleartext (http://, ws://) allowed by config or code.
Trusting user-installed certificates, or 'checking' a certificate by text that anyone can copy.
fixes: Keep the platform's default TLS checks; use HTTPS and WSS everywhere.
If you need more, pin the public key properly with the platform's pinning support.
Keep test proxies in debug-only configuration.

example.good: // leave the default certificate check in place

decoys.fix: Only switch off the certificate check for our own API host.
decoys.why: An attacker in the middle pretends to be exactly that host.

decoys.fix: Encrypt the request body with a key built into the app.
decoys.why: The key is in the app, so anyone can decrypt it, and headers and tokens still travel exposed.

decoys.fix: Check that the certificate's issuer name contains our company name.
decoys.why: Anyone can create a certificate with any issuer name.

signs: Logging request bodies, headers, PINs, BVNs, card data or tokens.
Crash reporting or analytics given full requests or user data.
'Debug only' logging that is also on in pilot, beta or support builds.
fixes: Log only what you need to investigate, and mask or drop sensitive fields.
Turn full logging on only in debug builds, and redact Authorization headers.
Treat log tools as places many people can read.

decoys.fix: Keep logs for 7 days instead of 90.
decoys.why: A week of PINs is still a breach, and log tools copy data elsewhere.

decoys.fix: Log at debug level instead of info.
decoys.why: Debug logs are often on in production, and the data is still written.

decoys.fix: Only let the support team read the logs.
decoys.why: Support doesn't need PINs, and the more people can read logs, the more ways they leak.

signs: JavaScript bridges (addJavascriptInterface, JavaScript channels) in WebViews that can load other sites.
URLs from links or intents loaded without strict checks.
Host checks done with contains, startsWith or endsWith on the URL text.
fixes: Parse the URL and compare the scheme and exact host with an allowlist.
Open anything else in the browser, not inside the app.
Expose the smallest bridge possible, and check the caller's origin in every method.

decoys.fix: Turn off JavaScript only on pages that don't need it.
decoys.why: The pages that use the bridge need JavaScript, and an attacker's page will run its own.

decoys.fix: Check that the URL contains our domain name.
decoys.why: evil.example/?x=ourdomain and ourdomain.evil.example both contain it.

decoys.fix: Rename the bridge to something hard to guess.
decoys.why: The name is in the app and in the page's JavaScript. Anyone can read it.

signs: Activities, services, receivers or providers with exported="true" (or an intent filter) and no permission.
Permissions with protectionLevel="normal", which any app can request.
Screens that return tokens or perform actions without checking who called them.
fixes: Don't export what other apps don't need (exported="false").
Protect what must be exported with a signature permission or a caller check.
Register runtime receivers as not exported.

decoys.fix: Give the action an unusual, hard-to-guess name.
decoys.why: Action names are in the manifest. Anyone can unzip the APK and read them.

decoys.fix: Check the intent has all the extras the screen expects.
decoys.why: An attacker sends exactly the extras you expect.

decoys.fix: Hide the component from the app's menus.
decoys.why: Other apps start it directly. Menus don't matter.

signs: Rules or policies like allow read, write: if true or using (true).
'Signed in' checks only (request.auth != null) on other people's data.
Public storage buckets for private files, or users able to edit their own role.
fixes: Check ownership in every rule: the record's owner must be the signed-in user.
Keep private files in private buckets and serve them through checks.
Never let users write fields that grant permissions.

example.good: allow read: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId;

decoys.fix: Only show other users' data in the admin screens of the app.
decoys.why: The database answers anyone who asks directly, whatever the app's screens do.

decoys.fix: Require users to sign in before reading.
decoys.why: Anyone can sign up in seconds. Signed in is not the same as allowed.

decoys.fix: Use hard-to-guess document IDs.
decoys.why: Rules that allow listing reveal the IDs, and IDs leak. Rules must check ownership.

signs: Secrets copied into images (COPY .env, ENV TOKEN=...) or left in a layer and deleted later.
Secrets printed in CI logs in a form masking doesn't catch (encoded, partial).
Build artifacts or uploads that include keystores, .env or config folders.
fixes: Pass secrets at run time, or mount them for one build step (Docker build secrets).
Never print secrets, in any form; check they're set without showing them.
Upload only the files a step needs.

example.good: # pass settings at run time: docker run --env-file .env ...

decoys.fix: Delete the file in a later RUN step.
decoys.why: Every step is a layer. The file is still in the earlier layer and can be extracted.

decoys.fix: Rely on GitHub masking secrets in logs.
decoys.why: Masking only matches the exact text. Encoded or partial secrets print in full.

decoys.fix: Make the container registry private.
decoys.why: Many people and systems can pull from it, and images get copied. The secret shouldn't be in the image at all.

signs: Scripts piped from the internet into a shell, especially over http.
Third-party actions or packages pinned to a branch or mutable tag, given secrets.
Untrusted input (pull request code, comments, package indexes) running in a privileged pipeline.
fixes: Pin third-party code to a full commit SHA or a verified version with a checksum.
Never run untrusted code or text where secrets are available.
Install from one package index you control.

decoys.fix: Download the install script over https instead of http.
decoys.why: That stops tampering in transit but you still run whatever the publisher (or whoever hijacks them) ships.

decoys.fix: Give the workflow only read access to the repository.
decoys.why: The untrusted code still sees the secrets passed to that step.

decoys.fix: Pin the action to a version tag like @v2.
decoys.why: Tags can be moved to new code. Only a full commit SHA is fixed.

signs: privileged: true, root users, host sockets or host paths mounted into containers.
Cluster-admin bindings, write-all tokens or Resource: "*" in policies.
Permissions wider than the job, 'just to make it work'.
fixes: Grant only the exact actions and resources the job needs.
Run as non-root, drop capabilities, and avoid host mounts.
Review permissions whenever a job's purpose changes.

decoys.fix: Keep the broad permissions but turn on audit logging.
decoys.why: Logs tell you after the damage. The permission is the damage waiting to happen.

decoys.fix: Only use the broad permission in production.
decoys.why: Production is where it matters most.

decoys.fix: Put the service in its own namespace.
decoys.why: A cluster-wide role or host access reaches across namespaces anyway.

signs: Backups, dumps, .env, .git or uploads under a web root or public bucket.
autoindex on, public bucket policies, or a web root set to the project folder.
Static file locations that skip the authentication other paths get.
fixes: Keep only public files in the web root; serve everything else through the app with checks.
Block public access on storage buckets and give jobs roles instead.
Deny hidden files and backups explicitly as a second line of defence.

decoys.fix: Turn off directory listing.
decoys.why: Files with guessable names (dates, .env, .git/config) can still be downloaded.

decoys.fix: Rename the backup folder to something hard to guess.
decoys.why: Folder names leak through scanners, logs and links. The files must not be public.

decoys.fix: Delete backups after 30 days.
decoys.why: Every one of those 30 days' files is public until then.
